subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: What is the lagoon behind Chesil Beach called?
back: The Fleet
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: Why do some geomorphologists call Chesil Beach a barrier beach rather than a true tombolo?
back: It was pushed landwards by rising sea level rather than built out by drift
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: About how long is Spurn Head spit?
back: About 3.5 miles (6 km)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: Where is the UK's largest active sand tombolo?
back: St Ninian's Isle, Shetland
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: About how long is the St Ninian's Isle tombolo?
back: About 500 m
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: Which sand spit shelters the mouth of the Exe estuary in Devon?
back: Dawlish Warren
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: According to the National Trust, about how long ago did sand begin to build the dunes at Studland, Dorset?
back: About 500 years ago
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: In 1999, how far was the Cape Hatteras lighthouse on the Outer Banks barrier islands moved inland?
back: About 2,900 feet (880 m)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: Why was the Cape Hatteras lighthouse moved in 1999, according to the US National Park Service?
back: Erosion had brought the sea within about 60 feet of the tower
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: Which US state's coast has the Outer Banks barrier islands?
back: North Carolina
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: Which Norwegian fjord is Norway's longest and deepest?
back: Sognefjord
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: About how long is the Sognefjord?
back: About 205 km
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: What is the maximum depth of the Sognefjord?
back: About 1,308 m
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: Which estuary in south Devon is a classic example of a ria?
back: Kingsbridge Estuary (Salcombe)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: In which country is the Dalmatian coast?
back: Croatia
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: On which Scottish island are King's Cave and raised beaches found near Blackwaterfoot?
back: Arran
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: Why does Scotland have raised beaches?
back: The land has risen by isostatic rebound since the ice sheets melted
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: According to a 2009 GPS study (Teferle et al.), about how fast is Edinburgh rising by isostatic rebound?
back: About 1 mm per year
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: According to a 2009 GPS study (Teferle et al.), about how fast is Lowestoft subsiding?
back: About 1.2 mm per year
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: Which former land area linking Britain to mainland Europe was drowned by rising sea level after the last glacial?
back: Doggerland (now under the North Sea)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: About how long ago did the Storegga submarine slide off Norway cause a tsunami in the North Sea?
back: About 8,150 years ago
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: According to IPCC AR6 (2021), how much did global mean sea level rise between 1901 and 2018?
back: About 0.20 m (20 cm)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: According to IPCC AR6, what was the rate of global sea level rise from 2006 to 2018?
back: About 3.7 mm per year
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: According to IPCC AR6, what was the rate of global sea level rise from 1901 to 1971?
back: About 1.3 mm per year
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: According to IPCC AR6, what is the likely global sea level rise by 2100 under the very high emissions scenario (SSP5-8.5)?
back: 0.63 to 1.01 m (relative to 1995-2014)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: According to IPCC AR6, what is the likely global sea level rise by 2100 under the very low emissions scenario (SSP1-1.9)?
back: 0.28 to 0.55 m (relative to 1995-2014)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: According to IPCC AR6, what is the likely global sea level rise by 2100 under the intermediate scenario (SSP2-4.5)?
back: 0.44 to 0.76 m (relative to 1995-2014)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: Why will sea level rise be greater than the global average in south-east England?
back: The land there is slowly sinking by isostatic adjustment
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.3 Coastal landscape development

front: In which year was the Mappleton coastal defence scheme on Holderness built?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.4 Coastal management

front: About how much did the 1991 Mappleton scheme cost?
back: About £2 million
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 1: Physical geography::Coastal systems and landscapes::3.1.3.4 Coastal management

front: What did the 1991 Mappleton scheme build?
back: Two rock groynes and a rock revetment

front: What is the geographical term for the growing interconnection and interdependence of the world's economies, cultures and peoples?
back: Globalisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: In globalisation, what is a flow of capital?
back: The movement of money across borders (investment, loans, aid, remittances)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is the difference between foreign direct investment (FDI) and portfolio investment?
back: FDI gives lasting control of a business, portfolio investment is buying shares or bonds only
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: In globalisation, what is a flow of labour?
back: The international migration of workers
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is the term for the emigration of highly skilled and educated workers from a country?
back: Brain drain
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Which flow of globalisation includes banking, insurance, tourism and call centres?
back: Flows of services
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Which flow of globalisation includes manufactured goods and raw materials traded between countries?
back: Flows of products (trade in goods)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Which flow of globalisation includes data, ideas and media sent through the internet?
back: Flows of information
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is offshoring?
back: Moving part of a company's own operations to another country
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is outsourcing?
back: Contracting another company to do part of the work, often in another country
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is global marketing?
back: Selling a product worldwide under a single global brand and image
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is the term for adapting a global product to suit local tastes and cultures?
back: Glocalisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is a supply chain?
back: The linked steps and companies that turn raw materials into a product for the consumer
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is the term for the system of supplying parts to a factory only when they are needed, cutting storage costs?
back: Just-in-time
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Which management system made popular by Japanese car makers aims to cut waste in production?
back: Lean production
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Who described the 'new international division of labour' (1980), with manufacturing moving to low-wage countries?
back: Fröbel, Heinrichs and Kreye
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: In the new international division of labour, where do TNCs usually keep headquarters and research?
back: In high-income countries
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: In the new international division of labour, where is routine assembly work usually located?
back: In lower-wage emerging and developing countries
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Traditionally, which group of countries dominated global consumption of manufactured goods?
back: High-income countries (Europe, North America, Japan)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How is the global pattern of consumption changing as emerging economies grow richer?
back: Consumption is rising fast in NEEs such as China and India
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How did containerisation act as a factor in globalisation?
back: Standard boxes cut loading time and shipping costs, making long-distance trade cheap
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Why can large container ships make trade with remote places more profitable?
back: Economies of scale lower the cost per unit carried
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How does air freight help globalisation?
back: It moves high-value, perishable goods such as flowers or electronics quickly
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Which communications technology carries most international internet data between continents?
back: Undersea fibre-optic cables
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How have communications systems such as the internet and mobile phones driven globalisation?
back: They allow instant, cheap contact and control of operations worldwide
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How did deregulation of financial markets act as a factor in globalisation?
back: Capital could move freely and quickly between countries
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How does electronic, 24-hour trading on stock exchanges help globalisation?
back: Money moves instantly between financial centres in different time zones
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How do security systems, such as encrypted online payments, act as a factor in globalisation?
back: They make e-commerce and international payments safe, so trade grows
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How do information systems such as barcodes and tracking help globalisation?
back: TNCs track goods along global supply chains in real time
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How do trade agreements act as a factor in globalisation?
back: They cut tariffs and quotas, so trade between members grows
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is a tariff?
back: A tax on imported goods
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is a quota in international trade?
back: A limit on the amount of a good that can be imported
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is the term for a barrier to trade that is not a tax, such as strict product standards?
back: A non-tariff barrier
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is free trade?
back: Trade between countries with no tariffs, quotas or other barriers
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is protectionism?
back: Using tariffs, quotas or subsidies to shield home industries from imports
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Which political and economic approach of the 1980s favoured free markets, privatisation and deregulation?
back: Neoliberalism
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Give an example of political globalisation.
back: Countries joining international organisations and treaties, such as the UN
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Give an example of social globalisation.
back: Spread of ideas and culture through migration, tourism and the internet
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Which US trucking businessman launched modern container shipping in 1956?
back: Malcom McLean
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What was the name of Malcom McLean's first container ship, which sailed in April 1956?
back: The Ideal X
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Between which two US ports did the Ideal X make its first container voyage in 1956?
back: Newark (New Jersey) to Houston (Texas)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How many containers did the Ideal X carry on its first voyage in 1956?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: According to UNCTAD, roughly what share of world trade by volume is carried by sea?
back: Over 80%
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Which container ship blocked the Suez Canal in March 2021?
back: The Ever Given
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: For about how long did the Ever Given block the Suez Canal in March 2021?
back: About six days (23 to 29 March)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Roughly how many ships were caught in the queue caused by the 2021 Suez Canal blockage?
back: Over 200
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What does the 2021 Ever Given blockage show about globalisation?
back: Global supply chains depend on a few chokepoints and are easily disrupted
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: According to the WTO, what was the value of world merchandise (goods) exports in 2024?
back: About US$24.4 trillion
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: According to the WTO, what was the value of world commercial services exports in 2024?
back: About US$8.7 trillion
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: According to the WTO, by about what percentage did services exports grow in value in 2024, compared with 2% for goods?
back: About 9%
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: According to UNCTAD's World Investment Report 2025, what was global FDI in 2024?
back: About US$1.5 trillion
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Which Swiss university's economic institute publishes the KOF Globalisation Index?
back: ETH Zurich (KOF Swiss Economic Institute)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Which three dimensions of globalisation does the KOF Globalisation Index measure?
back: Economic, social and political
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: In which year was the KOF Globalisation Index first published?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Which country ranked as the most globalised in the 2025 KOF Globalisation Index?
back: The Netherlands (Switzerland second)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Which Indian McDonald's burger is a well-known example of glocalisation?
back: The McAloo Tikki (potato-based, no beef)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is a global system?
back: A set of interconnected parts (states, firms, flows) working at a global scale
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is interdependence?
back: When countries rely on each other, so a change in one affects others
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is economic interdependence?
back: Countries relying on each other for trade, investment, jobs and supply chains
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is political interdependence?
back: Countries linked through alliances, treaties and international organisations
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is social interdependence?
back: Links between people in different countries through migration, culture and family ties
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is environmental interdependence?
back: Environmental change in one place has consequences for environments elsewhere
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Why are all countries environmentally interdependent?
back: They share global commons such as the atmosphere and oceans
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How can flows of FDI promote growth in a host country?
back: They bring jobs, skills, technology and tax revenue
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How can flows of remittances promote development?
back: Families spend them on food, housing, education and healthcare
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How can unequal flows of money cause inequality within a country?
back: Investment concentrates in a few cities or regions, widening the gap with rural areas
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: In global systems, what is an injustice?
back: Unfair treatment of people or places, such as exploitative pay and conditions
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How can global demand for resources cause conflict?
back: Groups or states fight over control of valuable resources such as oil or minerals
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Which sociologist developed world systems theory (1974)?
back: Immanuel Wallerstein
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: In Wallerstein's world systems theory, which three zones make up the world economy?
back: Core, semi-periphery and periphery
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: In Wallerstein's world systems theory, what is the core?
back: Rich states with high-skill, high-wage, high-tech production that dominate the system
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: In Wallerstein's world systems theory, what is the periphery?
back: Poor states supplying raw materials and cheap labour to the core
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: In Wallerstein's world systems theory, what is the semi-periphery?
back: States with features of both core and periphery, such as emerging economies
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: According to Wallerstein, how does the core benefit from the periphery?
back: Unequal exchange transfers wealth from periphery to core
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Who argued in 1967 that rich countries cause the 'development of underdevelopment' in poor countries?
back: Andre Gunder Frank (dependency theory)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What does dependency theory argue?
back: Poor countries stay poor because they depend on and are exploited by rich ones
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is neo-colonialism?
back: Control of poorer countries by richer states or TNCs through economic power, not direct rule
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is hegemony?
back: Dominance of one state over others through economic, military or cultural power
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is a superpower?
back: A state able to project its power and influence anywhere in the world
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is geopolitics?
back: How geography, power and politics combine to shape relations between states
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Who coined the term 'soft power'?
back: Joseph Nye
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is soft power?
back: Influence through attraction, such as culture and values, rather than force
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is hard power?
back: Influence through military force or economic pressure, such as sanctions
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How do powerful states drive global systems to their own advantage?
back: They set rules in bodies like the IMF, WTO and UN Security Council
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How can smaller, weaker states resist powerful states in global systems?
back: By forming blocs or alliances to bargain together
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Why are countries that depend on one primary export vulnerable?
back: A fall in its world price cuts export earnings sharply
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What do terms of trade measure?
back: The price of a country's exports relative to the price of its imports
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What does the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis argue about primary product exporters?
back: Their terms of trade tend to worsen over time against manufactured goods
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is the digital divide?
back: The gap between people with and without access to the internet and digital technology
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Why can a financial crisis in one country spread worldwide?
back: Banks and markets are interdependent, so losses pass between them
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Which US investment bank collapsed on 15 September 2008, deepening the global financial crisis?
back: Lehman Brothers
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How does the 2008 global financial crisis show economic interdependence?
back: A US housing and banking crisis caused recession around the world
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: In which year did China launch its Belt and Road Initiative?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Which Sri Lankan port was leased to a Chinese state company for 99 years in 2017 after debt problems?
back: Hambantota
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How many permanent members with a veto does the UN Security Council have?
back: Five
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Which country was suspended from the G8 in 2014 after it annexed Crimea?
back: Russia (the group became the G7)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Which coalition of developing countries at the UN was founded in 1964 to increase their bargaining power?
back: The Group of 77 (G77)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Which 1980 report drew a line dividing the rich 'North' from the poor 'South'?
back: The Brandt Report (the Brandt line)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Which oil exporters' cartel, founded in 1960, shows producer states using their power over a resource?
back: OPEC
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Since 1950, how has the growth of world trade compared with the growth of world output (GDP)?
back: Trade has grown faster than output
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: How has the share of world trade between developing countries (south-south trade) changed in recent decades?
back: It has grown rapidly
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is intra-firm trade?
back: Trade between branches of the same TNC in different countries
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a trading bloc?
back: A group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers between members
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a free trade area?
back: Members remove tariffs between themselves but keep their own tariffs on others
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What does a customs union add to a free trade area?
back: A common external tariff on imports from non-members
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What does a common (single) market add to a customs union?
back: Free movement of labour, capital and services
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a bilateral trade agreement?
back: A trade deal between two countries
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a multilateral trade agreement?
back: A trade deal among many countries, such as through the WTO
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is trade diversion?
back: Trade shifting from a cheaper outside supplier to a member of the same bloc
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a trade surplus?
back: When the value of a country's exports is greater than its imports
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a trade deficit?
back: When the value of a country's imports is greater than its exports
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is the term for higher tariffs on processed goods than on raw materials?
back: Tariff escalation
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: How does tariff escalation harm developing countries?
back: It discourages them from processing raw materials and adding value
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is added value?
back: The increase in worth of a product at each stage of processing
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: How do farm subsidies in rich countries harm farmers in poorer countries?
back: Subsidised crops are sold cheaply on world markets, undercutting them
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is dumping in international trade?
back: Selling exports abroad below the cost of production
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is preferential access in trade?
back: Lower or no tariffs for goods from particular countries, often the poorest
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is the WTO term for special rights that give developing countries more time and better market access?
back: Special and Differential Treatment
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: How can differential access to markets reduce a country's economic well-being?
back: Exports face high barriers, so jobs and income from trade are lost
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: How can access to a large market improve a country's societal well-being?
back: Trade income funds better health and education services
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: Why do landlocked countries often have weaker access to world markets?
back: They pay more to move goods through other countries to ports
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: Why can membership of a trade bloc be a risk for a smaller economy?
back: It becomes dependent on bigger members, so their recessions hit it hard
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What does Fairtrade guarantee producers?
back: A minimum price plus a social premium for community projects
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a transnational corporation (TNC)?
back: A company that operates in more than one country
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: Where are a TNC's headquarters and research usually located?
back: In its home country, often near universities
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: Why do TNCs locate manufacturing in emerging economies?
back: Lower labour costs and access to growing markets
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is vertical integration?
back: A TNC owning different stages of the same supply chain
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is horizontal integration?
back: A TNC buying or merging with firms at the same stage, often rivals
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a backward linkage for a TNC factory?
back: Local firms supplying parts or services to the factory
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is subcontracting?
back: A TNC paying another firm to make products or parts for it
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: Why do TNCs use subcontractors in low-wage countries?
back: To cut costs and avoid responsibility for running factories
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is transfer pricing by a TNC?
back: Setting prices between its own branches to move profit to low-tax countries
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What does it mean that a TNC is 'footloose'?
back: It is not tied to one location and can relocate easily
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is an Export Processing Zone (EPZ)?
back: An area offering tax breaks and few regulations to attract export industries
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is the 'race to the bottom'?
back: Countries cutting wages, taxes or regulations to compete for TNC investment
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is the multiplier effect of a TNC factory?
back: New jobs and spending create further jobs and income locally
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is profit leakage?
back: Profits made in a host country flowing back to the TNC's home country
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: Which positive impact of TNCs comes from training local workers?
back: Transfer of skills and technology
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What negative impact can a TNC have on its home country when it moves production abroad?
back: Factory closures and job losses (deindustrialisation)
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is global governance?
back: The rules, norms and institutions that regulate global issues without a world government
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: In global governance, what is a norm?
back: A shared expectation of how states should behave, such as respecting human rights
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is sovereignty?
back: A state's right to govern its own territory without outside interference
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Why does sovereignty limit global governance?
back: States can refuse to sign or obey international agreements
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What does it mean for a state to ratify a treaty?
back: To formally approve it, so it becomes legally binding on that state
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is an intergovernmental organisation (IGO)?
back: A body whose members are national governments, such as the UN
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is a non-governmental organisation (NGO)?
back: A non-profit body independent of government, such as Greenpeace
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What does it mean that global institutions 'reproduce' global systems?
back: Their rules keep the existing balance of power in place
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Why do critics say the IMF and World Bank favour rich countries?
back: Voting power depends on money paid in, so rich countries dominate
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What are IMF loan 'conditions' called?
back: Conditionality
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What were structural adjustment programmes (SAPs)?
back: IMF and World Bank loan conditions requiring spending cuts, privatisation and free trade
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Why were structural adjustment programmes criticised?
back: Cuts to health and education spending hurt the poorest people
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Which economist named the 'Washington Consensus' of free-market policies in 1989?
back: John Williamson
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is the main role of the IMF?
back: To keep the world financial system stable and lend to countries in crisis
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is the main role of the World Bank?
back: To lend money for development projects and to reduce poverty
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is the main role of the WTO?
back: To set trade rules, cut barriers and settle trade disputes between members
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is the WTO's most-favoured-nation principle?
back: A trade advantage given to one member must be given to all members
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Why can the WTO's dispute settlement process exacerbate inequality?
back: Poor countries lack the lawyers and money to bring cases
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Why is the UN Security Council veto criticised?
back: One permanent member can block action, even on humanitarian crises
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What are UN peacekeepers?
back: Troops from member states sent with consent to keep peace after conflict
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Why does global governance need action at the national scale?
back: National governments must pass laws to put global agreements into practice
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: How does local action link to global governance?
back: Local councils and people carry out policies, such as cutting emissions
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is the free-rider problem in global governance?
back: Some states benefit from others' action without contributing themselves
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is UNEP's role in global governance?
back: It coordinates UN environmental work and helps create environmental treaties

front: How can global agencies promote stability?

front: Which ocean areas are global commons?
back: The high seas, beyond countries' exclusive economic zones
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

back: The atmosphere

front: Which continent is treated as a global common?
back: Antarctica
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Beyond Earth, which area is a global common?
back: Outer space

subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Who wrote 'The Tragedy of the Commons' (1968)?
back: Garrett Hardin
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: What is the 'tragedy of the commons'?
back: Individuals each overuse a shared resource for their own gain, so it is destroyed
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Which economist won a Nobel Prize in 2009 for showing communities can manage commons sustainably?
back: Elinor Ostrom
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Why do global commons need global governance?
back: No single state owns them, so without rules they are overexploited
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: What does the 'common heritage of mankind' principle say?
back: Resources in some commons, such as the deep seabed, belong to all humanity
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: What is sustainable development, as defined by the 1987 Brundtland Report?
back: Meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Why does protecting the atmosphere conflict with developing countries' right to develop?
back: Cheap fossil fuels drive growth but add to global emissions
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: What does 'common but differentiated responsibilities' mean in climate agreements?
back: All states must act, but richer states that polluted more should do more
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: What is bioprospecting?
back: Searching wild species for genes or chemicals with commercial value
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: What does ABNJ stand for in ocean governance?

front: Why is Antarctica's climate so cold?
back: High latitude, high altitude and high albedo of ice

front: Why is Antarctica classed as a desert?
back: It receives very little precipitation, mostly as snow
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What are katabatic winds?

subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Why are temperatures on the Antarctic coast higher than in the interior?
back: Lower altitude and the moderating effect of the sea
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What is the difference between an ice shelf and sea ice?

front: Why does melting of floating ice shelves speed up sea level rise?
back: Shelves hold back land glaciers, which then flow faster into the sea
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: How does loss of sea ice speed up warming in Antarctica?

back: Less sea ice means less algae under the ice for young krill to feed on
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: How does ocean acidification threaten Southern Ocean species?

subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common
