back: India, China and Nigeria
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to the UN (WUP 2018), how many megacities were there in 2018?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to the UN (WUP 2018), how many megacities were projected for 2030?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to the UN (WUP 2018), which city was the world's largest in 2018?
back: Tokyo (about 37 million)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to the UN (WUP 2018), which city was the world's second largest in 2018, with about 29 million people?
back: Delhi
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to the UN (WUP 2018), which city was projected to become the world's most populous around 2028?
back: Delhi
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to the UN World Urbanization Prospects 2025, which urban area is the world's largest?
back: Jakarta (about 41.9 million)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to the UN World Urbanization Prospects 2025, which city is the world's second largest, with about 36.6 million people?
back: Dhaka
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to the UN World Urbanization Prospects 2025, what is Tokyo's rank among the world's largest cities?
back: Third (about 33.4 million)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to the UN World Urbanization Prospects 2025, what share of the world's 8.2 billion people live in cities?
back: 45% (using the new Degree of Urbanisation definition)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to the UN (WUP 2025), how many megacities were there in 1975?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to the UN (WUP 2025), how many megacities were there in 2025?
back: 33 (19 of them in Asia)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to the UN (WUP 2025), how many megacities are projected by 2050?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to the UN (WUP 2025), which city is projected to be the world's largest by 2050?
back: Dhaka (about 52 million)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: In the GaWC 2024 world city ranking, which two cities are the only ones in the top Alpha++ tier?
back: London and New York (London ranked first)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: Which US city, known as 'Motor City', is the classic example of deindustrialisation and urban decline?
back: Detroit
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: Which industry's decline caused Detroit's deindustrialisation?
back: The car (automobile) industry
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: In which year did Detroit's population peak, at nearly 1.85 million?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: What was Detroit's population in the 2020 US census?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: In which year did Detroit file for bankruptcy, the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: In which year was Shenzhen made one of China's first Special Economic Zones, triggering rapid urban growth?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: In which year were the first UK Urban Development Corporations set up, in London Docklands and Merseyside?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: When was the London Docklands Development Corporation wound up?
back: 31 March 1998
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to Hansard (1998), how much government grant did the London Docklands Development Corporation receive in total?
back: About £1.86 billion
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: According to Hansard, how did the population of the London Docklands development area change between 1981 and 1991?
back: It rose from about 39,400 to about 60,800
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: Which light rail line opened in 1987 to serve the regenerated London Docklands?
back: The Docklands Light Railway (DLR)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: In which year was the UK's City Challenge regeneration programme launched, with councils bidding competitively for funds?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: Which Manchester estate was regenerated under City Challenge from 1992, replacing the Hulme Crescents?
back: Hulme
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: In which year did the UK government merge regeneration funds into the Single Regeneration Budget?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: Which 1998 Labour programme gave 39 deprived neighbourhoods about ten years of funding for community-led regeneration?
back: New Deal for Communities
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: Which 1999 report by Richard Rogers' Urban Task Force called for an 'urban renaissance' on brownfield land?
back: Towards an Urban Renaissance
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: Which bodies replaced the Regional Development Agencies in England from 2011 to lead local economic growth?
back: Local Enterprise Partnerships (LEPs)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: What was New Islington in Manchester called before its Millennium Community regeneration?
back: The Cardroom estate
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: Which developer led the regeneration of New Islington, Manchester?
back: Urban Splash
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: Which New Islington apartment block, designed by Will Alsop and completed in 2009, looks like three stacked chips?
back: Chips
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.1 Urbanisation

front: What is meant by urban form?
back: The physical shape, size, density and layout of a settlement
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which physical factor explains why many cities grew at a bridging point or confluence of rivers?
back: Site and water supply (a wet point or crossing point)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: How does steep relief affect urban form?
back: It limits building, giving lower densities or growth along valleys
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: How does a coastline or estuary affect urban form?
back: It blocks growth on one side, giving a linear or semicircular shape
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which human factor gives cities a star-shaped or ribbon form?
back: Growth along main roads and railway lines
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which planning policy around UK cities stops outward urban sprawl?
back: Green belts
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What does CBD stand for?
back: Central Business District
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Why are land values highest in the CBD?
back: It is the most accessible point, so competition for land is greatest
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is the bid-rent theory?
back: Land users bid most for accessible central sites, so land use changes with distance from the centre
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which model of urban land use (1925) shows concentric rings around the CBD?
back: The Burgess model
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which model (1939) shows land use in sectors along transport routes?
back: The Hoyt model
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which model (1945) shows a city with several centres of growth?
back: The multiple nuclei model (Harris and Ullman)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: In the Burgess model, which zone around the CBD contains old factories and poor housing?
back: The zone in transition (inner city)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: In a typical LIC or NEE city, where are squatter settlements usually found?
back: On the periphery or on hazardous land such as floodplains and steep slopes
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Why do the rich in many LIC cities live near the centre, unlike in HIC cities?
back: The centre has the best services, jobs and security
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is social segregation in a city?
back: The separation of groups by income, ethnicity or class into different areas
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is meant by cultural diversity in a city?
back: The presence of people of many ethnicities, languages, religions and lifestyles
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is an ethnic enclave?
back: An area where one ethnic group is concentrated, with its own shops and institutions
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Why do new migrants often cluster in inner city areas?
back: Cheap rented housing and support from people of the same culture
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is a town centre mixed development?
back: A scheme combining shops, offices, housing and leisure in one central site
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is a cultural quarter?
back: An area of a city where arts, media and creative businesses are concentrated
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is a heritage quarter?
back: An area where historic buildings are conserved and reused, often for tourism
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is a fortress development?
back: A development designed to exclude outsiders, using walls, gates, guards and CCTV
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is a gated community?
back: A residential area with controlled entrances and boundary walls or fences
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is hostile (defensive) architecture?
back: Design such as spikes or sloping benches that stops homeless people resting
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which architect developed the 'defensible space' idea in 1972, linking design to crime levels?
back: Oscar Newman
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is gentrification?
back: Wealthier people moving into a poorer area, renovating property and displacing residents
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which sociologist coined the term gentrification in 1964?
back: Ruth Glass
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is an edge city?
back: A large concentration of offices, retail and leisure at the edge of a city, beyond the old centre
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which journalist defined the edge city in his 1991 book 'Edge City: Life on the New Frontier'?
back: Joel Garreau
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: In Garreau's definition, how does an edge city's number of jobs compare with its number of bedrooms?
back: It has more jobs than bedrooms
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Why are edge cities usually located near motorway junctions?
back: They depend on car access for workers and shoppers
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is the post-modern western city?
back: A fragmented, multi-centred city of varied architecture, consumption and segregated enclaves
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: How does the post-modern city differ from the modernist city?
back: It has many centres and mixed styles rather than one CBD and planned zones
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which US city is the model for the post-modern city studied by the 'LA School' of urbanists?
back: Los Angeles
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which writer described 'Fortress L.A.' in his 1990 book 'City of Quartz'?
back: Mike Davis
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What characteristic of megacities in LICs is shown by large informal settlements?
back: Rapid growth that outpaces formal housing supply
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is the informal economy?
back: Work that is not taxed, registered or regulated, e.g. street vending
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which business district just west of central Paris is often discussed as a European edge city?
back: La Défense
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which shopping-led mixed development opened in Liverpool city centre in 2008?
back: Liverpool ONE
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which shopping centre opened beside the London 2012 Olympic Park in 2011?
back: Westfield Stratford City
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which area of Manchester is known as a cultural quarter for street art and independent shops?
back: The Northern Quarter
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which Birmingham district is a heritage quarter based on its historic jewellery workshops?
back: The Jewellery Quarter
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which Sheffield area was one of the UK's first cultural industries quarters in the 1980s?
back: The Cultural Industries Quarter
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which gated suburb near São Paulo, begun in the 1970s, is a famous Latin American gated community?
back: Alphaville
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which tower, completed in 1991, was the first landmark office building of Canary Wharf?
back: One Canada Square
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: Which London industrial dock area became a second financial district from the late 1980s?
back: Canary Wharf (Isle of Dogs)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.2 Urban forms

front: What is economic inequality in a city?
back: Unequal distribution of income and wealth between people or areas
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: Which index combines income, employment, health, education, crime, housing and environment to rank deprivation in England?
back: The Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD)
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: What is the cycle of poverty?
back: Low income leads to poor housing, health and education, which keep people poor
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: How does economic inequality affect health in cities?
back: Life expectancy is lower in deprived areas
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: What is the difference between voluntary and involuntary segregation?
back: Voluntary is chosen to live with similar people, involuntary is forced by cost or discrimination
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: Which issue arises when ethnic groups live separately with little contact?
back: Lack of community cohesion, raising tension and mistrust
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: Which service pressure is linked to cultural diversity in cities?
back: Demand for translation, language teaching and culturally specific services
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: Which strategy reduces inequality by requiring new developments to include cheaper homes?
back: Affordable housing quotas
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: What is a living wage scheme?
back: Employers voluntarily paying a wage based on the real cost of living
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: What is in situ slum upgrading?
back: Improving services and housing in an informal settlement without moving residents
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: What is a site and service scheme?
back: Government provides plots with water, sanitation and roads, and residents build homes
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: What is the main weakness of relocating slum residents to distant tower blocks?
back: They lose access to jobs and social networks
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: Which strategy tackles cultural tension through laws on hate crime and discrimination?
back: Anti-discrimination legislation
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: What is the main weakness of area-based regeneration schemes for reducing poverty?
back: Poor residents move out or are displaced, so problems shift elsewhere
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: Why is the success of strategies to reduce inequality hard to measure?
back: Results take years, have many causes and depend on the indicator chosen
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: In which year was the London Living Wage first calculated by the Greater London Authority?
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: On what date did the Grenfell Tower fire in Kensington, London, happen?
back: 14 June 2017
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: How many people died in the Grenfell Tower fire of 2017?
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: Why is the Grenfell Tower fire used as evidence of urban inequality?
back: Social housing tenants died in one of the UK's richest boroughs
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: What strategic target does the London Plan (2021) set for the share of new homes that are affordable?
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: Which Rio de Janeiro programme from 1994 upgraded favelas in situ with roads, water and sanitation?
back: Favela-Bairro
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: Which is often described as Rio de Janeiro's largest favela?
back: Rocinha
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: Which street in Tower Hamlets is the centre of London's 'Banglatown' Bangladeshi community?
back: Brick Lane
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: Which annual London festival, held since 1966, celebrates Caribbean culture?
back: Notting Hill Carnival
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: Which body was set up in 1995 to run Mumbai's slum rehabilitation scheme, rehousing residents in flats on site?
back: The Slum Rehabilitation Authority (SRA)
point: 3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.3 Social and economic issues associated with urbanisation

front: What is the urban heat island effect?
back: Urban areas being warmer than the surrounding countryside
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Which amateur meteorologist first described London's heat island in 'The Climate of London' (1818 to 1820)?
back: Luke Howard
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: At what time of day is the urban heat island usually most intense?
back: At night
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Which weather conditions give the strongest urban heat island?
back: Calm, clear anticyclonic conditions
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Why do concrete, brick and tarmac add to the urban heat island?
back: They absorb and store heat by day and release it slowly at night
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: How does low albedo of dark urban surfaces add to the heat island?
back: Dark surfaces reflect less and absorb more solar radiation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What is anthropogenic heat?
back: Heat released by human activity, e.g. vehicles, industry, heating and air conditioning
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Why does less vegetation in cities raise temperatures?
back: Less evapotranspiration, so less energy is used as latent heat
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: How do street canyons trap heat?
back: Tall buildings reflect radiation between walls and reduce the sky view for heat loss at night
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: How does a pollution dome affect urban temperatures at night?
back: It absorbs and re-radiates outgoing longwave radiation back down
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Why does rapid drainage of rainwater raise urban temperatures?
back: Less surface water is left to evaporate and cool the city
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: On a temperature cross-section, what is the sharp rise in temperature at the rural-urban edge called?
back: The cliff
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: On a temperature cross-section, where is the peak of the urban heat island?
back: Over the dense city centre (CBD)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What are parks and lakes called on an urban temperature cross-section, where temperatures dip?
back: Cool islands (sinks)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: How does the urban heat island affect snow cover in cities?
back: Snow falls and lies less often than in the countryside
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: How does a green roof reduce the urban heat island?
back: Plants cool the roof by evapotranspiration and shading
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What is a cool roof?
back: A roof with a high-albedo (light) surface that reflects sunlight
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Roughly how much more rainfall do large cities receive than surrounding rural areas?
back: About 5 to 15% more
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: How does the rough surface of a city increase rainfall?
back: Buildings cause turbulence that forces air to rise
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: How does the urban heat island cause thunderstorms?
back: Strong convection lifts warm moist air, forming cumulonimbus clouds
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: In which season and time of day are urban thunderstorms most common?
back: Summer, in the late afternoon and early evening
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Why does urban pollution increase precipitation?
back: Particulates act as condensation nuclei for water droplets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Why were fogs more frequent in industrial cities before clean air laws?
back: Smoke particles acted as hygroscopic nuclei for condensation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Why is fog now less frequent in many city centres than in nearby countryside?
back: The heat island keeps air above its dew point and pollution is lower
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: How does the rough urban surface affect average wind speed?
back: Friction from buildings reduces average wind speed
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What is the venturi effect in cities?
back: Wind is squeezed and accelerated through gaps between tall buildings
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What is the canyon effect on urban wind?
back: Wind is channelled along streets lined by tall buildings
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What happens to wind that hits the face of a tall building?
back: It is deflected down the building, causing strong gusts at street level
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What forms on the sheltered (lee) side of tall buildings?
back: Eddies and vortices with turbulent, swirling air
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: How does urban layout affect wind direction at street level?
back: Buildings divert wind along streets, so local direction differs from the regional wind
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What is a country breeze?
back: A light inflow of cooler rural air towards a warm city centre on calm nights
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What are particulates?
back: Tiny solid or liquid particles suspended in air, e.g. soot and dust
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What does PM2.5 mean?
back: Particulate matter less than 2.5 micrometres across
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Why is PM2.5 more harmful than larger particles?
back: It penetrates deep into the lungs and bloodstream
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Which source produces much urban particulate pollution in HIC cities?
back: Road traffic, especially diesel exhausts, plus brake and tyre wear
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Which pollutants react in sunlight to form photochemical smog?
back: Nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Which secondary pollutant is the main component of photochemical smog?
back: Ground-level ozone
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: In what weather conditions does photochemical smog form?
back: Hot, sunny, calm anticyclonic weather
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: How does a temperature inversion worsen urban air pollution?
back: Warm air above cooler air stops pollutants rising and dispersing
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Why are cities in basins, such as Mexico City and Los Angeles, prone to smog?
back: Surrounding mountains trap air and inversions are frequent
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What is a congestion charge?
back: A daily fee to drive into a city's central zone, reducing traffic and pollution
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What is a low emission zone?
back: An area where the most polluting vehicles pay a charge or are banned
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What is one weakness of number-plate driving bans?
back: Wealthier people buy a second car to get round them
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: How does a catalytic converter reduce urban pollution?
back: It converts carbon monoxide, NOx and hydrocarbons into less harmful gases
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: In which month and year did the Great Smog hit London?
back: December 1952
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: According to the Greater London Authority, about how many excess deaths did the 1952 Great Smog cause at the time?
back: About 4,000 (later studies estimate about 12,000)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Which UK law was passed in 1956 in response to the Great Smog?
back: The Clean Air Act
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What did the Clean Air Act 1956 introduce in UK cities?
back: Smoke control areas where only smokeless fuels could be burned
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: On what date did London's Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) start in central London?
back: 8 April 2019
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: On what date was London's ULEZ expanded to the North and South Circular roads?
back: 25 October 2021
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: On what date was London's ULEZ expanded to cover all London boroughs?
back: 29 August 2023
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: As of November 2026, what is the daily ULEZ charge for a non-compliant car in London?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: In which year did London introduce its Congestion Charge, at £5 a day?
back: 2003 (February)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What did London's daily Congestion Charge rise to on 2 January 2026?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: In which year did Mexico City start the 'Hoy No Circula' scheme banning cars on one weekday by number plate?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: When did Delhi first run its odd-even scheme for private cars?
back: 1 to 15 January 2016
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: According to IQAir's World Air Quality Report 2024, which was the world's most polluted capital city?
back: New Delhi
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: What annual PM2.5 guideline did the WHO set in 2021?
back: 5 µg/m³
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: In which year did a lorry blown over by wind near Bridgewater Place tower in Leeds kill a pedestrian?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Which Leeds tower became the UK's best-known example of dangerous wind tunnelling at street level?
back: Bridgewater Place
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.4 Urban climate

front: Why does urban surface runoff increase compared with rural areas?
back: Impermeable surfaces such as tarmac and roofs stop infiltration
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: How do drains and sewers change water movement in an urban catchment?
back: They carry water rapidly to rivers, shortening travel time
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: Which drainage basin store is greatly reduced by urbanisation?
back: Soil and groundwater storage (also interception by vegetation)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: How does urbanisation affect groundwater recharge?
back: Less infiltration and percolation reduce recharge
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is channelisation?
back: Straightening, deepening or lining a river channel, often with concrete
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is a culvert?
back: An enclosed channel or pipe that carries a river underground
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is the effect of urbanisation on the lag time of a flood hydrograph?
back: It shortens the lag time
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is the effect of urbanisation on peak discharge?
back: It raises peak discharge
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What shape is the rising limb on an urban storm hydrograph?
back: Steep
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What happens to the falling limb on an urban storm hydrograph?
back: It is steep, as water drains away quickly
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: How does urbanisation affect a river's base flow?
back: It lowers base flow because less water reaches groundwater
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is a combined sewer?
back: A sewer carrying both rainwater and sewage in the same pipe
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is a combined sewer overflow (CSO)?
back: A release point where sewage and stormwater spill into rivers when sewers are full
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is surface water (pluvial) flooding?
back: Flooding when intense rain overwhelms drains before reaching a river
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: How does urban runoff affect river water quality?
back: It carries oil, metals, litter and sediment into rivers
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What are SUDS?
back: Sustainable urban drainage systems that mimic natural drainage by storing and slowing runoff
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: In the SUDS triangle, what is the third aim besides water quantity and water quality?
back: Amenity and biodiversity
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is the SUDS management train?
back: A sequence of techniques from source control through site to regional control
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: How does a green roof work as a SUDS technique?
back: Plants and soil on the roof intercept and store rain, slowing runoff
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: How does permeable paving work as a SUDS technique?
back: Rain soaks through gaps into a gravel layer below instead of running off
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is a swale?
back: A shallow, grassed channel that carries, slows and infiltrates runoff
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is a detention basin?
back: A dry grassy hollow that fills briefly in storms and releases water slowly
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is a retention pond?
back: A permanent pond that stores runoff and lets pollutants settle
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is a soakaway?
back: An underground pit filled with rubble that lets water infiltrate into the soil
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is a rain garden?
back: A planted hollow that collects roof or road runoff and lets it soak in
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is a filter strip?
back: A gently sloping strip of grass that slows runoff and traps sediment
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: How do water butts reduce urban runoff?
back: They store roof water for reuse instead of sending it to drains
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is one environmental benefit of SUDS beyond flood control?
back: They create wildlife habitats and green spaces
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is one weakness of permeable paving?
back: Its gaps clog with silt and need regular cleaning
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: Why are infiltration SUDS unsuitable on clay soils?
back: Clay has low permeability, so water cannot soak away
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: Why should infiltration SUDS not be used on contaminated land?
back: Infiltrating water could carry pollutants into groundwater
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is one economic weakness of retrofitting SUDS into existing cities?
back: Space is limited and installation is costly
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is river restoration?
back: Returning a damaged river towards a more natural state and function
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is de-culverting (daylighting)?
back: Opening up a river that was in an underground culvert
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: Why does re-meandering a straightened river reduce flood risk downstream?
back: A longer, rougher channel slows water and increases lag time
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: How does reconnecting a river to its floodplain reduce urban flooding?
back: The floodplain stores floodwater temporarily
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: Why are weirs removed in river restoration projects?
back: To let fish migrate and restore natural flow and sediment movement
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is one way of evaluating the outcome of a river restoration project?
back: Measuring changes in flood frequency, water quality and species numbers before and after
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is one common conflict in urban river restoration projects?
back: Restoration needs land wanted for housing or other uses
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: On what date in 2007 did Hull suffer major surface water flooding?
back: 25 June 2007
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: According to the University of Hull, how much rain fell on Hull in 24 hours on 25 June 2007?
back: About 110 mm
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: According to the Independent Review Body, how many households were affected by the Hull floods of June 2007?
back: Over 8,600
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: How many businesses were affected by the Hull floods of June 2007?
back: Over 1,300
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: How many people died in the Hull floods of June 2007?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What did the Independent Review Body conclude was the main cause of the 2007 Hull floods?
back: The drainage system was overwhelmed (not river flooding)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: Which residential development in Cambourne, Cambridgeshire, is a well-known UK SUDS monitoring scheme?
back: Lamb Drove
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: Which conventionally piped site was used as the control when Lamb Drove's SUDS were monitored from 2008 to 2011?
back: Friar Way
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: According to the Lamb Drove case study, how much did SUDS save on construction costs compared with a traditional scheme?
back: About 10%
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What did Lamb Drove monitoring find about water leaving the SUDS site compared with piped drainage?
back: Its water quality was better
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: In which year did Copenhagen adopt its Cloudburst Management Plan after severe flooding in 2011?
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: According to the EEA, how much damage did Copenhagen's 2011 cloudburst cause?
back: More than DKK 6 billion
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: Which south-east London river was restored through Sutcliffe Park in a scheme reopened in 2004?
back: The River Quaggy
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: Which government agency led the River Quaggy restoration at Sutcliffe Park?
back: The Environment Agency
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: Which local campaign group pushed for the River Quaggy to be restored rather than further culverted?
back: Quaggy Waterways Action Group (QWAG)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What happened to the River Quaggy in Sutcliffe Park during the restoration?
back: It was brought out of its culvert into a meandering channel
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: How was Sutcliffe Park reshaped to reduce flood risk downstream in Lewisham?
back: The park was lowered to act as a floodplain that stores floodwater
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: According to QWAG, how much did the Sutcliffe Park regeneration cost?
back: About £3.8 million
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: Which Seoul stream was uncovered by removing an elevated highway, reopening in 2005?
back: Cheonggyecheon
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: Which Seoul mayor led the Cheonggyecheon restoration?
back: Lee Myung-bak
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Case studies and evidence::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.5 Urban drainage

front: What is municipal solid waste?
back: Waste collected by local authorities, mainly from households and small businesses
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: Name one source of urban industrial and commercial waste.
back: Construction and demolition (also: manufacturing, offices, shops)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: How does waste per person change as incomes rise?
back: It increases
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: How does the composition of waste in HICs differ from LICs?
back: HICs have more plastic, paper and metal, LICs more food and organic waste
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: What is a waste stream?
back: The flow of a type of waste from its source through to its disposal
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: How do attitudes affect recycling rates?
back: Environmental concern and convenience raise people's willingness to sort waste
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: Why are recycling rates often lower in flats than houses?
back: There is less space for bins and collections are harder
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: What is unregulated waste disposal?
back: Dumping or burning waste without controls, e.g. fly-tipping or open dumps
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: What is one environmental impact of unregulated open dumps?
back: Leachate pollutes water and burning releases toxic smoke
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: What is one social benefit of informal waste picking in LIC cities?
back: It provides an income for the urban poor and recycles materials
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: What is the main environmental advantage of recycling?
back: It saves raw materials and energy compared with making new products
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: What is one disadvantage of recycling?
back: Contaminated loads are rejected and end up in landfill or incineration
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: What is meant by waste recovery?
back: Getting value from waste, e.g. energy, compost or biogas
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: What is anaerobic digestion?
back: Breaking down food waste without oxygen to make biogas and fertiliser
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: What is energy from waste?
back: Burning waste in an incinerator to generate electricity or heat
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: By roughly how much does incineration reduce the volume of waste?
back: About 90%
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: What is one advantage of incineration over landfill?
back: It generates energy and takes up far less land
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: Which toxic pollutants are a concern from waste incineration?
back: Dioxins and fine particulates (also toxic fly ash)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: What is the carbon cycle impact of incinerating plastics?
back: It releases fossil carbon to the atmosphere as CO2
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: Why are incinerators said to 'lock in' waste?
back: Long contracts need a steady supply of waste, reducing pressure to recycle
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Contemporary urban environments::3.2.3.6 Urban waste and its disposal

front: What is the main greenhouse gas produced by landfill sites?

front: How many schools were closed because of smoke from the Deonar landfill fire in 2016?
